utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, you may sit down, but could you also give us the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. We are the 15th of March, 2007 today. I would like to greet the accused and all the people in this courtroom. We must resume our hearing and bring in the next witness, but before we do that, do we have an IC number, registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. [In English] Several parties have submitted documents lists of documents to be tendered through Witness DE. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number 486. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 487. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 488. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 489. The OTP has also submitted a supplemental list of documents to be tendered through witness Marijan Biskic. That list will be given Exhibit number 490. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. First of all, as far as the hearing dates in July and August are concerned, the Trial Chamber had set the dates from the 7th of July to the 7th of August. The Prosecutor told us in writing that there was a problem at the beginning of August and that we might face a technical problem, matters relating to photocopying of documents, so we discussed this yesterday and decided to postpone it by a week, which means that the -- we will end on the 13th of August, which is a Friday. In fact, it will be on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we shall resume on the 13th of August at quarter past 2.00. This is a decision the Trial Chamber has taken regarding the schedule. Now, as far as Mr. Karnavas's intervention yesterday is concerned, the Chamber is deliberating, and in the next few days we shall hand down a decision which undoubtedly will be an oral decision. For the time being, we have not entirely taken our decision, and we are in process of taking it, and we shall keep you informed as soon as we have taken our decision. That said, I am personally looking into the question that was raised. Not so much and -- as a matter of form than content, namely Rules 44 and 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I shall certainly hand down a decision personally. I feel that as a Judge, and in light of the powers I have been given, I am entitled to put any question at any time. In addition, as far as Mr. Scott is concerned, I noticed yesterday on several occasions that you said that if you'd had enough time you would have done this and that. Of course, I -- this got me thinking, and in the night I did my calculations, and I'd like you to pay attention to what I'm about to say. In this trial you wish to tender into evidence 10.000 documents. If a -- if it takes us six minutes per document on average, let's say six minute per document, 10.000 documents multiplied by 6, so that's 60.000 minutes. If I divide this by 60 to calculate the number of hours, we're talking about -- we will reach something like a thousand hours to look into the documents, which would amount to 250 trial days solely dedicated to the review of documents. So obviously we will not have time to review all the documents you wish to tender into evidence. Therefore, in its wisdom, the Trial Chamber has permitted you to tender these documents by means of a written motion so that you tender those documents which you feel to be the most important. Obviously there will be some questions you will not be able to put because you cannot tender all the documents. That goes without saying. But every time you say you don't have time, you don't have time. One cannot compare a trial where a thousand documents are being presented with a trial where there might be something like 20 or 30.000 documents. As a matter of interest, I looked at the Blagojevic -- Blagojevic trial this morning. 800 documents had been presented by the Prosecution, 170 by the Defence team during the cross-examination, which has nothing to do with the figures we're talking about here at this trial. We therefore have to apply a rational working method. One cannot apply the same rules in this case, and you cannot apply the rules which apply to a previous trial to this particular trial. If that were the case and if I do want to refer you to the Blagojevic trial, in that trial the accused weren't even entitled to put any questions. So those 10.000 documents unfortunately cannot all be presented at trial, and I think you need to be well aware of that. You need to present the most important documents. I know that with the upcoming witness we have a number of documents which you went to -- which you wish to tender through the witness, and thanks to the 92 ter Rule, you will be entitled to present these documents. This is Witness L. Protective measures have been granted, i.e., closed session. We discussed the matter as to whether there should be distortion of the face and of the voice and whether he should be heard or she should be heard in closed session. We felt this person could be easily identified, so we decided to hear this witness in closed session. Usher, please bring the blinds down and ask the witness to come into the courtroom. Yesterday, we also discussed the question of time, how much would be granted to each party. We reviewed the content of the documents, and in light of this Mr. Petkovic would have 40 minutes, Mr. Praljak 40 minutes, Mr. Prlic 40 minutes also, because his name is mentioned in one of the documents similarly, and the three other accused would have 20 minutes. But, of course, if you so wish, you can give your time to somebody else. That's for you to decide. In broad terms, this is how we have shared out the allocated time. That said, as we don't have much time, sometimes if you give your time to somebody else this might be difficult to substantiate, but this will have to be addressed on a case-by-case basis. The Prosecution will have one hour all in all and no more. So, Mr. Flynn, please make sure that you present your documents in that space of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I want to make sure that you can understand me in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been granted protective measures, which means that your testimony will be heard in closed session. Nobody can hear what you are saying, but for the purpose of this procedure -- these proceedings I need to have your date and place of birth, please. We need to move into closed session. I thought this was automatic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you press the button and raise the blinds. Mr. Scott, the planning for next week, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't looked at the exact count, but we -- the Prosecution anticipates calling a number of fact witnesses next week. It looks like about -- about seven, approximately seven witnesses next week, many of whom we hope can be presented fairly briefly. Yes, that's all I would say about it. I'm not going to mention particular names because there may be protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you're saying seven, then there must be 92 ter witnesses among them. I have already said that the 92 ter procedure consists of an admission of documents and written testimony. Of course you know that, a few documents directly linked to this 92 ter witness. That's the meaning of this procedure. If the procedure is used to do direct examination, then this is a different procedure altogether. I know that there is no perfect jurisprudence in this area, but as I attend the Plenary meetings of Judges, when this provision was introduced, and I was one of the authors, was to speed up the procedure which would admit the -- which would allow for the admission of documents but which would also allow the Defence to cross-examine, so that that was the main purpose. However, I note that your practice has been slightly different. You ask questions about documents, and then you show a large number of documents to these witnesses, whereas the purpose of this procedure has, in a sense, been changed. As you are telling us you are calling seven witnesses, I assume there won't be so many documents, especially documents that can be shown to other witnesses, as was the case with this witness. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. We certainly agree that one of the main purposes behind Rule 92 ter was to allow more evidence to be taken in a written form more quickly and more efficiently. Having said that, and as you know, having been a member of the Rules Committee who drafted the rule, it was in fact also part of the purpose, and is stated in front of -- face of the Rule in part A to allow the direct examination to be taken in whole or part, part viva voce, part in writing, or one or the other, altogether. It has been the Prosecution's position since many months ago in the trial as the Chamber will recall that we should in some instances be allowed to conduct what we would -- might call a mixed examination, some based upon putting in the statement, some based upon viva voce testimony, which is the practice followed in most Chambers with -- to good effect, because it does save time on those portions which are not put viva voce. So it is a time saving method. Otherwise, Your Honour, we are put in a position of an all or nothing choice. We would have to put the entire evidence in viva voce or the entire evidence in 92 ter, which is not what 92 ter contemplates, because further in 92 ter A, it says that a Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness. But be that as it may, I thought next week's witnesses will not involve -- I don't think any single of those witnesses will indeed involve a large number of documents. We will continue to try to find our way applying 92 ter as best we can, given the jurisprudence and given what the rule says. I would just -- if that completes -- there's one other point I wanted to address, Your Honour, if that complete's Your Honour's comments on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will give you the floor, but let us complete the discussion on 92 ter. I have taken note of what you have said, and I agree with you that this -- this is a procedure that allows time to be saved and in the decision we have said that this has a -- procedure has allowed to save 45 hours in relation to the time envisaged if those witnesses were to come to testify viva voce. So it is an important saving of time, and I fully agree with you. And this procedure, of course, may be used by the Defence if they so wish for their own witnesses. So I give you the floor as you wish to touch on other points and we have time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just very briefly. Just to confirm on that last point again, as we've said before, of course from day one, in fact going back to the pre-trial portion of this case, we had always anticipated making maximum use of what has since become 92 ter. It used to be Rule 89(F). But that has always been the intention of the Prosecution to use the Rule to the maximum extent that we thought reasonable and indeed save as much time as possible. Your Honour, I just wanted to come back -- I didn't want to leave the week with an error on the record or a misunderstanding. At the beginning of the week the Chamber addressed the matter of when the Prosecution had made a filing concerning the contact that Mr. Pusic had with the witness -- with the witness in Mostar and had some comments about that. Just so the record is clear, Your Honour, there was never a motion filed. There were several references to the fact that the Prosecution made a motion. In fact, the Prosecution didn't make a motion. In fact, the Prosecution didn't ask for any action to be taken whatsoever. It was simply filed for the information of the Chamber. It may be -- there may be a base -- a request for action in the future but there was simply nothing for the Chamber to deny. There was no request for action by the Prosecution but simply to inform the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two points in connection with what you have said. I come back to 92 ter because in line 9 you say that 92 ter replaced 89(F). Unfortunately, I don't have the Rules in front of me, but I don't think that 89(F) has been redacted. I may be wrong. My impression is that that Rule -- that Rule has been maintained. It's still there. I have the Rules. Which means, Mr. Scott, in theory, that one can also refer to 89(F) again, which has been used in other cases. So you also have means, I would almost say a boulevard, a highway before you if you wish to use 89(F) as it has already been used. Having said that, a second point: You're coming back to the Pusic case. I take note that for you this was just for the sake of information for the Chamber, and the Chamber rendered an oral decision regarding the filings. I didn't have time to present another argument. I wanted to say that if in the future you find yourself confronted with this situation is to immediately inform the other party about it. And the second rule is that before the hearing to let us know, rather than putting us before a fait accompli, because last time we were placed exactly in such a position, and you explained that you had been working for 14 hours that day, which I can understand. Therefore, that's all I wish to point out. My colleague also wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm and to state the Chamber was perfectly aware of the fact that it was not seized by a motion of the Prosecution or any other party, and I -- I'm very sorry if the formulation of the oral decision could give rise to a misunderstanding. I would regret this, but I can assure you that we were perfectly aware of the procedural situation as you have correctly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I appreciate that. It may have been a translation error, or it may not just been an a casual use of a term. I'm pretty confident the transcript will reflect on Monday that references were made to a motion filed by the Prosecution but I'm certainly not going to belabour it. I don't think there was a fait accompli. I think the information was provided to the Chamber for the Chamber's only information sake. There may or may not be times in the future where it would not be appropriate for the Prosecution to bring that immediately to the Chamber's attention because there may be additional investigation that the Prosecution would conduct. So the Prosecution is mindful of these matters. We are indeed very concerned about anything that possibly interferes with a witness and, apart from advising the Chamber, we may seek action ourselves by enlisting the assistance of local law enforcement or international organisations in the area to seek to address these matters. So it may or may not be appropriate to bring it immediately to the attention of the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour. Yesterday I made some comments with respect to the previous day and with respect to the previous day, and with respect to what I believe is the procedure that is universal more or less throughout this Tribunal, except with this Trial Chamber with respect to asking questions. And I want to clarify my position and I do so with all due respect because of certain comments that, Mr. President, you've made in my -- in my opinion which are not necessarily helpful in these matters. You stated such as, "I want you to know -- I want to know if you mind me asking a question. If I may, with your permission, without accusing me of undermining your rights. You're not going to reproach me for asking a question. I should have asked my question straight away but this displeases the Defence so I prefer to wait," and so on. Now, I understand there seems to be perhaps some confusion as to what exactly I'm trying to convey to the Trial Chamber, so let me go slow. Let me be methodical about this. First and foremost, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence has ever said that the Trial Chamber is not allowed to ask questions. Obviously the Rules provide for that. In fact, they provide that you can ask questions at any time. What we have said -- or what I have said is that the practice in this Tribunal has been to allow the Prosecution, if they're going first, to put on their direct examination, followed by cross-examination by the Defence, followed by questions by the Bench, and then to allow the parties, the Prosecution and Defence, to ask any follow-up questions with respect to any questions posed by -- by the Bench, and yesterday there was a good example. At the conclusion of General Praljak's questioning, you asked a question. It was relevant. It was pertinent. And after that General Praljak asked to -- to have a moment to -- to put another question and indeed his question was a follow-up to your question, and it all tied in and it made sense. That's the preferred procedure. Now, I'm not suggesting that this be -- that this is a rigid procedure. My preference is, if there is some sort of a misunderstanding, if there is a point that needs clarification, it should be done right on the spot. I don't have a problem with that. If I'm moving from a chapter, from a particular topic, normally I it turn to Your Honours if you have a question to follow up on that as opposed to waiting to the end. That's my approach. I think it helps. Where the problem arises and I'm saying this because I wish you to understand the dilemma that I am facing, because we spend a lot of time trying to fit in a lot of information that what convinced period of time. If I pull out a document and before I've been given an opportunity to at least address the points I think are necessary and important in the document and you begin to ask questions, because obviously you have your questions in mind you're entitled to those questions, but if you do that, sometimes you go in a particular direction that maybe -- that I may need to go there but -- or maybe I wasn't intending to go there, but now, because of the limited time that you've given me, it throws us off, and it is frustrating. And so I want to make sure that you understand that I'm not saying that you can't ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to allow you to continue it. You're quite right. Maybe it's a misunderstanding. I fully agree with what you have just said, and I have no different opinion on this point and I'll tell you why, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So this is the -- the problem that we're having and the Prosecution is having this problem as well, we have a lot of documents. Last week -- I'll be very concrete. There was an objection -- there was an intervention. I would like to say it was an objection by Judge Trechsel when I put a document in. It had to do with this particular Spider operation. I didn't go into that. There was a -- there was a very correct observation made by Judge Trechsel. The problem is if I don't have time to go in and develop that because I have limited period of time, I have to move on. Hopefully when I finish the chapter you will understand at least the point that I'm trying to make and in that instance we will have other witnesses who will follow up on that. I can assure you that at least on this side, and I'm sure on that side as well, we really work very hard to try to figure out what points we need to make, how we're going to make them, and in -- the order in which we need to make them. On direct examination they need to tell a narrative. They need to tell a narrative so at least their side of the story gets out and then we are able to challenge that story, if necessary. So if that narrative is not presented in a way that we can challenge it, they're going to have a problem at the end of the case. We have a problem challenging it. And all I'm saying, Mr. President, is if you would at least trust us, because I think we're professional, trust us, we will get you there. I am not opposing to you asking as many questions as you want, but at least allow me the -- allow me the opportunity to develop the point and if -- if you need to ask a particular question because you -- you think this is important, fine. I've never suggested, nor will I ever suggest, that you're not entitled to ask questions. And I understand the Rule. You can ask them whenever you wish. I'm just saying sometimes you're -- there seems to be some impatience, and with some cross-examination, if it's a difficult witness, you cannot be direct with the witness. If you're too direct you're never going to get anything out of them. And if we tell you in advance and the witness hears it, then there goes the surprise. So I just want to make sure that there's no -- we haven't -- you know, that there's no misunderstanding on what I'm trying to convey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree with what you have said. There's no divergence of views regarding the substance of your statement, and of course we will respond in legal terms to what you have said, but rest assured that you enjoy our trust. I should like to quote two points which occurred, and due to lack of time I myself did not ask a question, and I'll explain which those points are. I remember it was a few months ago, I know, that you were not here because -- there was a co-counsel who was present. I think it was Madam Nozica who produced a document between Tudjman and Izetbegovic regarding the recognition by Tudjman and Izetbegovic of the HVO as an army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, a very important document, and this document emerged in the course of a cross-examination, and we didn't really look into all the consequences of that document. Was that document addressed to the UN Secretary-General as it was a treaty of cooperation between two countries? Was that document published in the Official Gazette, et cetera, et cetera. There was a series of questions that could be put, but due to lack of question I didn't do so. Perhaps you will come back to that document at some point, but at the time I had the impression that we were going very fast, and I could have put questions and I didn't. A second point, and it has to do with Mr. Coric's Defence. A document appeared very quickly and the document came from the military police and the author of this document indicated that Tuta's men were carrying out ethnic cleansing in Mostar. So this military policeman was sending a report to his high authority, and I said to myself here we have the military police telling us about something that they did not take part in. I wanted to intervene and ask questions. If I had intervened, perhaps Mr. Coric's Defence would have said we'll talk about this document later and so on, but due to lack of time I didn't intervene. I could have. And I hope those two documents will reappear one day. If they do not through the Defence of any of the accused, the Prosecutor will not come back to them. And as the Judges have tens of thousands of documents, we might forget this, and this would be prejudicial. So when we intervene, it is because we are trying to reach the truth. And on another point, I was not in agreement with you yesterday when you said that this was an adversarial procedure, but there's the truth of the Prosecution, your truth, and the Judges who have to establish what the truth, with a capital T, actually is, and that is why we must try through our questions to complement certain facts. And my feeling is, and I've already said, that in 90 per cent of the cases, 95 per cent of the cases, most of those questions are in favour of your clients. I will finish with another example. It has to do with the Defence of Mr. Praljak. One day an expert witness on sniping was here. We see the photographs, et cetera. And I myself asked to see the photos again because I saw that there was another point that could have been fired at, and neither party had noticed this, and that is why I wanted the photos to be seen again. Perhaps Mr. Praljak would have done that later on, I don't know, but I said it was important for him if I do that now. So you see, many questions are in favour of the Defence. And when you say that it is not a totally fair trial, I would like you to tell me of another Chamber that is to such an extent in favour of the rights of the Defence. And if you ask us to apply the same proceedings as other Chambers, I can tell you that we have allowed the accused to put questions. You know that in the Blagojevic case the accused could not ask questions. We have allowed the accused to choose their own lawyers. We have rendered a series of decisions in favour of the Defence. And when you say that one might be prejudicial, believe me, that is really painful. That hurts, especially in view of the way in which we're working. And there may be some misunderstanding between us, but I wanted to point this out. Of course you are right regarding the threat of sorts, and we will endeavour to allow you to develop your arguments during your examination so you will be satisfied, but there are moments when one needs to intervene because one might feel at a certain moment that there's something that needs to be raised. Another example. There was Mr. Pusic's witness. He was apparently said to have been present in a detention area, in a place of detention, and this witness said this. I asked this witness -- Mr. Pusic is here, and I asked him, do you recognise him? And the witness said no. Should I not have said that? Should I not have asked that question? I have a witness who says that Pusic is there and I ask him, is he here, and he says no. So I am trying to convey to you that through our questions we are endeavouring to establish the truth, and very frequently the result of the questions can be in your favour. If you wish to take the floor again, you're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. I have -- I believe Mr. Murphy wishes to comment something about, I guess, the quest for the truth. I suspect that -- that's his topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just conscious that Mr. Karnavas has carried much of the burden of speaking for all of the accused and I think part of that is his -- his liking to take the initiative in these matters and speak frankly to the Court. We were not -- I was not anyway aware that he was going to make this particular address yesterday to the Court so I didn't really have time to consider what my response to that would have been, but having thought about it overnight and obviously I will express it in a slightly different way, I think that part of the problem that -- that there is here is this: Is something that Your Honour just pointed to about the nature of these proceedings and to what extent, if at all, they are adversarial and I think what we have here to some extent is a sort of clash of cultures between the adversarial and the inquisitorial procedures and we're all struggling to find a way to -- to make this hybrid system fair in the interests of all the parties, and clearly that's not an easy thing to do. But I have to say, Your Honour, that right from the earliest days of the Tribunal when President Cassese first of all made his speech introducing the Rules of Procedure and Evidence on the 11th of February, 1994, he did make it clear that the Judges at that time had deliberated and had decided to lay down what they called an essentially adversarial proceeding or form of trial, I should say, mode of trial. And even though we've had a number of amendments to the Rules of Procedure since then and even though time constraints have made subsequent Presidents to make slightly different pronouncements on that point, it does remain an essentially adversarial procedure to this extent, that the Prosecutor from day one of the Tribunal's life has gone out and done investigations in the adversarial system, following adversarial modes, which means the Prosecutor's concern is to develop other own case, not to try and develop the Defence's case. That's always been our responsibility. And so we have never had on the Defence side the range of protections that come with the inquisitorial system it. For example, in France I know -- I'm sure in Switzerland, which I'm less familiar with, there is a highly developed series of protections for the accused given the nature of the investigation. For example, the use of the Zuznostruks [phoen], perhaps not -- I don't know, Your Honour, in Switzerland, but certainly in many civil law countries. But we simply don't have those protections. The protections that we have on the Defence side are those that are appropriate for the adversarial system that depend on having the right to investigate independently and to develop our own case through cross-examination, and one of the results of that, which I know is frustrating to the Judges, is that you don't always -- you can't always see where the Defence is going and when Your Honour says well we're putting questions which are in favour of the Defence, I know that's Your Honour's intention but with all due respect you don't necessarily know whether -- perhaps they are in favour of the Defence and perhaps not. The other thing, Your Honour, that does trouble me as a lawyer who has worked in the adversarial system for many years, and I think probably troubles my colleague from that system, is when Your Honour says that there's the truth of the Prosecution and your truth and the truth with a capital T, I can't help getting the message that somehow those of us who work in the adversarial mode are not committed to -- to ensuring the fairness of a trial or trying our best to bring out the truth. Your Honour, rightly or wrongly we do believe that the adversarial process is one that is well suited to bringing out the truth because when the parties go head to head and present their cases the truth has a way of emerging from that. Maybe not in the most direct way, such as the inquisitorial system has, but our experience over years and centuries of that has been that it is effective, and I -- I do once again very respectfully remind Your Honours that in these trials and like in all criminal trials the ultimate issue is not truth with a capital T, which is inherently unattainable, it's whether the Prosecution has proved the guilt of these accused beyond reasonable doubt of certain allegations that have been made and if the Defence establishes a reasonable duty and even perhaps all of us go away from the courtroom at the end of the day feeling, well, we're not really sure what happened, we're not sure that we ever did get to the bottom of this because of the complexity of the issues and the number of documents and the unreliability of certain witnesses; nonetheless, the law says that in that situation the accused would be entitled to be acquitted. And, Your Honour, our goal on the Defence said I know it can be presented sometimes in a cynical way but it's not meant in that way. It's meant to simply assist the Court to establish whether there is a reasonable doubt because as we see it that's the -- I know that Your Honour doesn't mean to disparage the adversarial system but sometimes certain observations by the Trial Chamber could be understood in that way, and I do remind Your Honours very respectfully that because of the protections offered to the Defence, this has to be an essentially adversarial system, because the fair -- the essential proceedings to protect the accused, the essential safeguards of fairness which Your Honours use in the inquisitorial system simply are not present in the mode of trial in this Tribunal. And, Your Honour, I think when Mr. Karnavas draws attention to the -- his desire to conduct his cross-examination in a free and uninhibited way he's not in any sense denying the Court its proper role. He's simply saying that within the adversarial system the right of cross-examination and to confront the witness is -- is probably the most fundamental protection given to the accused and it's given under an Article 21 of the Statute, and, Your Honour, it's simply that point that we're respectfully making to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a point of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I suspect this is about the thing you were asking for, Mr. Karnavas, this kind of discussion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely, Your Honour, because I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So -- yeah. Thank you. That means we can go to the weekend without having starting to draft a letter of resignation for lack of ability, as you have, not quite politely, I must say, suggested that we should do. But, excuse me, it's a point of order. We have already within the Chamber discussed about all these problems, and we have come to the conclusion that we would not wish to discuss this further today because we are in a very weak position as far as manpower is concerned. We're just half of the power or two-thirds, and it is not -- simply not fair, I think, to go on with this in the absence of at least Judge Prandler, who is also a full-fledged voting member of the Chamber. That is why I have interrupted at this point. This means that I myself refrain also from commenting that I do not invite the Prosecution to -- to comment, to certainly have their say on this but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be good for my colleagues to speak up at this point and then at least your colleagues on the Bench could have those thoughts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- thoughts together, and then we can revisit this issue but I think it might be useful, and I'm sure Mr. Scott is extremely talented and can speak off-the-cuff if he needs to with respect to his role in these proceedings, if he wants to speak today or wait until some other point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar is telling us that we just have a few minutes left. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't take the floor yesterday, and I had two reasons for that. The first is the one mentioned by Mr. Murphy. I didn't know that we would be discussing the matter. And the second reason is my personal reason, and I present my own personal views. I also -- I, of course, respect Mr. Karnavas's possession and my colleagues but, Mr. President, I've been before you for three or four years now. I had a trial before that and I have had a very positive experience with what you did and how you conducted the proceedings there. So I have my own personal view and position and that's how I'm going to present my view, my colleagues, of course, have the right to present their views.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I won't take up much time but I'd like to say two things. Today we have heard that about 95 per cent of the Judges' questions is something that goes to the benefit of the Defence. I have to say for principled reasons that I consider that a exceptionally worrying matter and cause for concern, to say that 95 per cent of the questions go to the benefit of the Prosecution, if you were to say that, we would all be on our feet and up in arms, and I'm worried about this 95 per cent that you say is to the benefit of the Prosecution but also anything to the benefit of the Prosecution which can be of such importance that they can have a vital influence on the decisions. So this brings us to the matter of a fair or unfair trial. Now, with respect to the obligation of Judges to seek for the material truth, to seek material truth, I completely agree with what was said today here by Mr. Murphy, my colleague, and I'd just like to remind you that the Defence of Mr. Petkovic has repeatedly said that it is not the truth that is to be decided but the circumstances which will determine the responsibility and accountability of the accused. I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that this is a topic, that is to say the obligation on the part of the Judges to seek for material truth. We coming from the area of the former Yugoslavia are very well-versed in that method because all the procedure and rules in the former legal system made it incumbent upon the Judges to seek material truth and regardless of the disposition of the parties in the proceedings decide upon the evidence that is going to present -- be presented and the facts that they consider to be material in making their rulings. We in Croatia considered that when we changed these procedural matters and rules and regulations and with the -- or alleviated the burden from the Judges in seeking material truth considered that we had made a democratic step forward and allowed the parties in the proceedings to make decisions which, in a criminal procedure, means if the Prosecutor has failed to prove the indictment then the accused should be set at liberty. I do not consider it necessary to add anything to what I've already said and I would like to say that I completely agree with what my colleagues said before me and if we are going to have a debate and discussion on the issue in due course then I will prepare more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you. As you know, the Chamber will continue to deliberate and decide whether we're going to have a separate meeting devoted to these specific problems. It is 1.00. I'm going to adjourn the hearing and we reconvene at 2.15 on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.02 p.m.
